headlines.article_text: Anthropic IPO live updates: ANT stock price and Nasdaq debut Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu watch now VIDEO 5:16 05:16 Anthropic raises $81B+ in historic IPO: Here's what to know Squawk Box Anthropic is set for its long-awaited Nasdaq debut on Thursday, after the artificial intelligence lab raised over $81 billion in a record IPO , surpassing SpaceX 's offering in June. The Claude creator sold 980 million shares at $83 a piece on Wednesday, lifting the size and price of its offering. Its fully diluted market cap sits at around $1.5 trillion. Tune in at 10:00 a.m. ET as Dario and Daniela Amodei join CNBC TV exclusively to talk about the debut. Watch in real time on CNBC+ or the CNBC Pro stream The 5-year-old company captivated the corporate world with its Claude AI models and products, which have fueled its meteoric rise this year. Anthropic said in its prospectus that it generated $33.24 billion in revenue for the nine months ended Sept. 30, up a staggering 1,200% from the same period last year. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei co-founded the company in 2021 after he and a small group of researchers defected from OpenAI , now its chief rival. Anthropic has faced sharp criticism over its positions on safety, regulation and national security, including by President Donald Trump and other senior government officials. The company will list on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol "ANT," and its debut will be a big test for the AI industry. Investors have been fretting over Jensen Huang's sudden ouster at Nvidia , voters' stinging rebuke of AI during the midterm elections and the feasibility of a multitrillion-dollar infrastructure buildout . "Our aim is to help humankind chart a safe course through this technological evolution, open new frontiers of discovery, and bring forth an age of miracles," Anthropic's co-founders wrote in the company's prospectus. "Everyone who owns our stock, whether an institution or an individual, becomes part of that effort." Anthropic targeted retail allocation of about 20%, as CNBC previously reported, a much higher percentage than the typical initial public offering, which is 5% to 10% for retail investors. Anthropic's stock could trade into the low $100s on Thursday, according to the people, who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to speak publicly. — Ashley Capoot 41 Min Ago Over 400 Anthropic employees set to become centimillionaires watch now VIDEO 2:18 02:18 Anthropic's IPO could mint thousands of millionaires — and reshape San Francisco Tech The average Anthropic employee will be worth over $40 million after today's IPO, marking one of the most rapid wealth creation events in history. The AI lab has generated 1.77 billion employee options. Earlier hires stand to benefit even further, with over 400 employees expected to be worth $100 million or more at the current share price. Lockup periods may alter the timeline for the gains to make it to the economy, but the newfound wealth is expected to supercharge the San Francisco real estate market and philanthropic giving. — Robert Frank, Caleigh Keating 39 Min Ago Here's what it's like outside the Nasdaq Outside the Nasdaq ahead of the Anthropic IPO on Nov. 19th, 2026. Ashley Capoot | CNBC As of around 8:00 a.m. ET, the scene outside the Nasdaq is pretty sleepy, though there is some police presence. The Nasdaq isn't promoting Anthropic's logo yet, but there are some ads for Elon Musk's Grok Bot and the neocloud Nebius . — Ashley Capoot 1 Hour Ago Amodeis arrive at the Nasdaq Dario Amodei, chief executive officer of Anthropic PBC, and his wife Camilla Clark arrive for the Anthropic PBC initial public offering (IPO) at the Nasdaq MarketSite in New York, US, on Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026. Adam Gray | Bloomberg | Getty Images Daniela Amodei, co-founder and president of Anthropic PBC, arrives for the Anthropic PBC initial public offering (IPO) at the Nasdaq MarketSite in New York, US, on Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026. Adam Gray | Bloomberg | Getty Images Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and his sister, Anthropic President Daniela Amodei, have arrived at the Nasdaq in New York City. — Ashley Capoot 1 Hour Ago Anthropic IPO to surge 25% when it opens, perpetual futures indicate Anthropic PBC signage ahead of the company's initial public offering (IPO) at the Nasdaq MarketSite in New York, US, on Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026. The futures in Anthropic on the Hyperliquid exchange were trading above $104, indicating a surge of more than 25% from its $83 IPO price. Anthropic trading in so-called perp futures on Polymarket were also showing a jump to similar levels. "Early indications are that it's up about 25%," said J.J. Kinahan, senior VP of retail and alternative investments at CBOE Global Markets, on CNBC "Squawk Box." "With some of the tumultuous times here for Nvidia, a little bit of that trust has gone away from the retail investor so this is the way people I think are going to express themselves." Perpetual futures are a crypto-based new type of futures contract which never expire and don't represent any ownership in the companies its tracking. The derivatives correctly predicted the initial pop in the SpaceX IPO back in June. Retail investors are clamoring to buy Anthropic in the open market, according to Vanda Research. Elon Musk's company ended up raising a total of $85.7 billion after underwriters exercised their overallotment. headlines.article_text: Walmart (WMT) Q3 2026 earnings Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Walmart narrowly topped fiscal third-quarter earnings and revenue estimates and raised its full-year sales and earnings outlook. In an exclusive interview with CNBC, CEO John Furner said Walmart has been working to keep prices low despite soaring diesel costs. The company highlighted e-commerce sales growth as it said it saw success with store-fulfilled pickup and delivery. In this article WMT Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 6:49 06:49 Walmart CEO John Furner on Q3 results: Customers continue to look for value Squawk Box Walmart on Thursday reported earnings and revenue that narrowly topped estimates and raised its full-year outlook as it saw strong e-commerce growth ahead of the busy holiday season. Walmart said global e-commerce sales grew 17%, driven by store-fulfilled pickup and delivery, with Walmart U.S. up 23% and Sam's Club U.S. rising 30%. Its Walmart U.S. advertising business saw a 37% sales increase for the quarter. Walmart said it rolled back prices on nearly 8,000 products across its stores, a focus as U.S. consumers worry about the cost of living in the face of elevated food and gas prices. CEO John Furner told CNBC's Becky Quick that the company has seen higher-than-expected diesel costs, but that tariff refunds have helped the retailer to offset those inputs and maintain lower prices. "The reality is that increases in diesel fuel and transportation, they do work their way into cost of goods," Furner said in an exclusive interview. "So we're hoping to see these costs come down as soon as possible, and we'll keep prices as low as we can." CFO John David Rainey told CNBC that growth in online orders for Walmart and Sam's Club was driven by an emphasis on speed of delivery and reduced prices. He added that Walmart saw its largest share gains in the food category in three years during the third quarter. "This was another really solid quarter for us, we feel good about it," Rainey told CNBC. "We continue to gain share while continuing to improve the profitability of our digital businesses." Shoppers enter a Walmart store in Charlotte, North Carolina, Aug. 30, 2026. Travis Dove | Bloomberg | Getty Images Walmart also raised its full-year guidance, now expecting net sales to rise between 4.9% and 5.2%, compared to previous guidance of a 4% to 5% increase. Rainey said Walmart is maintaining "flexibility" in its guidance. Walmart anticipates adjusted earnings per share will come in between $2.84 and $2.89, compared with a prior range of $2.80 to $2.87. It's also now expecting adjusted operating income to increase between 8% and 8.6%, up from the previous outlook of between 7% and 8.5% growth. Here's how the company performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG: Earnings per share: 65 cents adjusted vs. 64 cents expected Revenue: $188.84 billion vs. $187.27 billion expected For the quarter ended Oct. 31, the company reported net income of $4.95 billion, or 62 cents per share, down from $6.14 billion, or 77 cents per share, the year prior. Revenue rose 5.2%. Walmart U.S. recorded net sales of $125 billion, up 3.6% from the year prior. Its comparable sales excluding fuel rose 2.9%, in line with Wall Street expectations, according to StreetAccount. Furner also said Walmart is seeing encouraging adoption of its artificial intelligence agent, named Sparky, especially ahead of the holiday season. He said it's led to customer basket increases of 40% on average. "It just is a great way of just completing the entire basket and solving entire the solution for people," he said. Sam's Club reported net sales of $25.9 billion, marking a 10% increase from the year-ago period. It said its sales were driven by strength in the grocery category and general merchandise. In October, Walmart announced it was launching a joint membership option with Walmart+ and Sam's Club as it leans further into convenience. Both stores will still offer standalone memberships, as well. Furner told CNBC the new membership has brought roughly two million new people into Sam's Club since its launch in late October. Though the company reimbursed some members for the new membership rate, Rainey added it's already seeing positive returns on the joint model and that consumers are "spending appreciably more." The company on Thursday said its global membership fee revenue grew 17% in the third quarter. The company is typically well-insulated from macroeconomic pressures because of its value reputation. Last quarter , the company said it was lowering prices of products across multiple categories, including beef. Rainey said on Thursday that he's "optimistic" about consumer spending heading into the holiday season and that the fourth quarter is already "off to a pretty good start." The big-box retailer has posted solid growth over the past few quarters as it sees customers gravitate to reduced prices, improvements in delivery and gains in its advertising business. It's also leaned into attracting higher-income consumers with its Walmart+ membership. Shares of Walmart have fluctuated this year but are up roughly 13% year-to-date.
